then.text: Marjory Tulloch. Soup, bannocks, a pot of tea. The chart? Gone, is it? Well. Goodness. Tragic. More tea?
I've not been near the museum in weeks. Weeks. Mind the counter, there's a lot of paper under it. Napkin stock. Ahem.

ls_tea_lady.text: Soup, bannocks and a pot of tea strong enough to stand a spoon in. The Shetland bannock is a soft round loaf, cooked on a girdle, good with butter and jam. We do a lot of reestit mutton soup in winter, if you're after something proper.
Reestit mutton is mutton that's been salted and hung to dry in the rafters, the old way. In the soup it's wonderful. It is also, I'm told, an acquired taste. The acquiring takes about one bowl.

ls_soup_fan.text: Fish tea, we called it when I was a lad. Not tea, mind. A fish supper with the tea. The boats came in, the fish were boiled with tatties, and everyone sat down. That was it. It was glorious.
Now we've got tasting menus. I had a lamb the size of a thumb on a plate the size of a hat. I paid thirty pounds and went home for a sandwich.

then.text: She is still on. Five days. In March she broke down and we had a charter for three weeks, which cost more than the engine. I do not say it is an argument. I say it is a fact.
Three days. I have the crew on part-time and the old girl has two years left in her. I am proud of her and I am not blind.
The little new one is a fine boat. I will not say otherwise. She is not mine, and she is not hers, and the sheep go by charter. I have gone into the harbour office and been very civil.
Whatever the isle asks, I will sail what I am given. I have never had a boat I did not love, and I have had some I should not have.
Tell Eila I will be at the meeting, and I will keep my mouth shut, which is not like me.

else.text: Magnie Tulloch. Twenty-six years on the isle boat, and fourteen before that on worse. She is old, but she is sound.

The council would cut my days, and the crew with them. I would be lying if I said I did not mind. I would also be lying if I said the boat was not dear to run. Everyone has seen the figures. I have seen them upside down, across a desk.
What I will say is this: a boat that carries sheep, a doctor and a coffin is not a bus. It is how the isle stays an isle and not a holiday cottage. Whatever else you hear, hear that.
Soup, a roll and the weather forecast. In that order. Do not talk to me before the forecast.

then.text: That was yours. The rest of the mailbag is for the isle, and the isle can wait for its tea.
There you are. A letter for you, off the boat. Eila put it in with the post for Lerwick and told me not to let it fall in the harbour.
Dear {player}. The committee voted for the full boat. The council found the money by putting off a road scheme in the north Mainland, and the north Mainland wrote a number of letters to the paper.
The boat runs five days. In March the old engine failed and we had a charter for three weeks, which cost more than the engine. The old boat will need replacing in any case.
I think we bought time. Time is what a small place needs most, and what it is always asked to give up first. Come and see the isle. The boat will take you. It is still allowed to.
Dear {player}. Three sailings a week: Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday. The vet comes on Tuesday and the nurse on Thursday, and nobody is ill on a Wednesday, by agreement.
The school bairns board in Lerwick Monday to Friday, which some did anyway and which Lorna hates. Two families left in the autumn. I will not say it was the boat, and I will not say it was not.
The old boat has two more years in her, Magnie says. After that we shall all have a conversation we have been avoiding. Come on a Tuesday. We are best on a Tuesday.
Dear {player}. A new little boat, from the spring: twelve passengers, faster, with a heated cabin, which has been a revelation. Nobody has been sick in it, which is a first for the isle.
It will not carry sheep. The sheep go on a charter twice a year, and the crofters mutter, and rightly. The council kept the flight for emergencies.
We have a boat. We have fewer things the boat can do. I think that is what a fair answer is, in a place like this. Come in the spring. Bring the wind.

And a shawl, folded small enough to pull through a ring, Eila says, so it will go in your bag. And a note on how to do stovies. The isle way, it says, with the dripping. You will not get it from a book.

else.text: Nothing off the boat yet. It comes when the boat comes, and the boat comes when it can. Try after a night's sleep.

w55k_skipper.text: The new boat. Twelve passengers, a heated cabin, and a very clean deck. I came in from the mainland ferries and I have not stopped being surprised that people wave.
I know about the sheep. I have been told, by a number of crofters, in a number of tones. I intend to learn the tone before the lambing.
